title: The Cyborg and the Companion Species: Denver, New Haven, and the Redwoods Above the Pacific
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Denver, born in the last September of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and city (UCSC Special Collections finding aid, Donna Jeanne Haraway Papers, ark:/13030/c8b283b2); the day, 6 September, comes from the ISFDB bibliographic entry rather than a vital record. No birth certificate or newspaper notice was reached.
stops.campa: Donna Jeanne Haraway is born in Denver in the last September of the war. The household is Catholic, Irish on her mother's side, and the parish supplies the shape of the week. She will say later that the eucharist taught her before any theory did that a sign and a body can be the same thing, that matter and meaning do not sit in separate departments. Asked where her figures come from, she starts there, with the parish and the wafer, and not with any book she read afterward.
suggested_refs: The UCSC finding aid to the Donna Jeanne Haraway Papers, UA 42, whose date range opens in 1966 and leaves the childhood undocumented
sources: UCSC Special Collections finding aid, ark:/13030/c8b283b2
Wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', citing Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: Cherry Hills Village, the nuns at St. Mary's Academy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia, citing How Like a Leaf pp. 8-9, places her high schooling at St. Mary's Academy in Cherry Hills Village, a municipality separate from Denver; the research pool wrongly gave the place as Denver. The date orders the segment only. The Mass-for-dolls, the closet confessions, and the considered convent vocation come from How Like a Leaf alone, first person and undocumented elsewhere.
stops.campa: The nuns teach her. She reads Aquinas at thirteen, and the faith she will later call a deep apostasy is at this point a vocation she is seriously turning over. The academy stands in Cherry Hills Village, not in Denver proper, a few miles south of the house. What she takes from the years there is a technique rather than a doctrine: a figure is an operative thing and not a decoration, and a small ceremony does work in the world. By her own account she says Mass for her dolls, and hears their confessions in a closet.
suggested_refs: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf (Routledge, 2000), pp. 8-9, the only source for the dolls and the vocation
sources: Wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', citing How Like a Leaf pp. 8-9
Muriel Lederman's Isis review, cited in Wikipedia for the Catholic formation

stops.name: Denver, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the year is an ordering device. The sources give an age, not a date: Wikipedia, citing How Like a Leaf pp. 6-7, says Dorothy died of a heart attack when Haraway was sixteen. Born 6 September 1944, that places the death between September 1960 and September 1961. The research pool's 1960 is a plausible pick, not evidence. The maiden name is spelled Maguire in the pool and Mcguire in Wikipedia; neither was settled by any document reached.
stops.campa: Her mother dies of a heart attack. Haraway is sixteen. The sources give the age and not the date, so the year has to be reasoned backward from a birthday, and even the maiden name comes down in two spellings. What is clear is the shape it leaves: the daughter of a Catholic household loses the person the household ran on, in the middle of the years when the vocation is still an open question. Thirty years later she dedicates Simians, Cyborgs, and Women to her mother, and prints the dates on the page.
suggested_refs: The dedication page of Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991), which carries Dorothy's dates
sources: Wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', citing How Like a Leaf pp. 6-7
Haraway, dedication in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991)

stops.name: Colorado Springs, the Boettcher scholarship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The full-tuition Boettcher Foundation scholarship is attested (Wikipedia, citing How Like a Leaf pp. 12, 175), but no source reached gives a matriculation year: the Wikipedia article contains none, and the Colorado College honorary-degree records were not fetchable. 1962 is back-calculated from the 1966 degree.
stops.campa: A Boettcher Foundation scholarship covers the whole tuition and sends her sixty miles south to Colorado College. She takes zoology for the major and philosophy and English for the minors, and refuses to rank them, a refusal she is still making fifty years later when people ask whether she is a scientist or a critic. She is eighteen. Colorado Springs sits at six thousand feet, one mountain range and one parish away from the house in Denver, with Pikes Peak standing over the campus all winter.
suggested_refs: The Boettcher Foundation scholarship records for Colorado, which fix the tuition award but not the year
sources: Wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', citing How Like a Leaf pp. 12, 175

stops.name: Colorado Springs, the degree in zoology
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1966 B.A. in zoology with minors in philosophy and English (Wikipedia); the month is an ordering device. The 1986 honorary Doctor of Science is tagged [R]: the Colorado College recipient list was cited in the research pool but could not be fetched.
stops.campa: She graduates with a bachelor's degree in zoology and minors in philosophy and English, a combination nobody advised her into and nobody at the time had a name for. She has learned to dissect and she has learned to read philosophy, and she does not treat these as two separate skills. Twenty years on, the college will call her back and give her an honorary doctorate of science, among its first to its own alumni. For now she has a laboratory training and a reading list in metaphysics. A Fulbright application is already in the post.
suggested_refs: The Colorado College honorary-degree recipient list, which records the 1986 DSci at Opening Convocation
sources: Colorado College honorary-degree recipient list, cited in the research pool, not fetchable

segments.name: Paris and New Haven: The Organism as a Philosophical Problem

stops.name: Paris, the Fondation Teilhard de Chardin
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance, inferred as to year, approximate as to pin. Wikipedia states she moved to Paris and studied evolutionary philosophy and theology at the Fondation Teilhard de Chardin on a Fulbright; the UCSC finding aid independently adds the Universite de Paris. Neither gives a year, so 1966-67 is inferred from the degree. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate, since no source reached fixes the Fondation's premises.
stops.campa: The Fulbright puts her in Paris to study evolutionary philosophy and theology at a foundation carrying the name of a Jesuit paleontologist, a man who spent his life arguing that matter and spirit were one process running forward. The archive at Santa Cruz records the University of Paris on the same fellowship, so she is enrolled in two places at once. She is twenty-two, out of a zoology bench in Colorado and into a room where the standing question is whether evolution is going anywhere in particular.
suggested_refs: The Fondation Teilhard de Chardin, then attached to the Museum National d'Histoire Naturelle, whose premises no source reached fixes
sources: UCSC Special Collections finding aid, ark:/13030/c8b283b2, 'Fulbright Fellow at Universite de Paris and Fondation Teilhard de Chardin'

stops.name: Paris, the war heard in another language
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Haraway's own recollection, relayed through the research dossier, that she first encountered the Vietnam and Indochina war through French politics shortly after Algerian independence. No source reached fixes a month; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Algeria has been independent four years and the French left is still arguing about it in every cafe and every newspaper. Haraway hears the American war in Vietnam described in a vocabulary with no American equivalent: as Indochina, as a colonial war with a history running long before Washington entered it. She has arrived a Catholic scholarship student from Colorado and is being handed, in a foreign language, the frame she will use on her own country for the rest of her life. Nothing in the Fulbright paperwork accounts for this part of the year.
suggested_refs: The French press of 1966-67 on Indochina and on Algeria four years after independence
sources: Haraway's own recollection, relayed in the research dossier; not independently fetched

stops.name: New Haven, the doctoral programme in biology
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia gives the entry into Yale's biology doctoral programme in 1967; the research pool itself tags this claim [R] and no registrar record was reached. The month is an ordering device. Haraway's line about Hutchinson's circle and cybernetics comes from an interview with Nicholas Gane which neither the research pass nor this one fetched, so it is used unquoted.
stops.campa: She enters the biology doctoral programme at Yale and lands in the orbit of G. Evelyn Hutchinson, the limnologist whose students are permitted, encouraged even, to read philosophy on the department's time. Haraway will later say that Hutchinson's circle was deeply interested in cybernetics, herself included. The field Norbert Wiener had named at MIT two decades earlier is already ordinary conversation in the laboratories where she is learning to do developmental biology. She is twenty-three and registered as a biologist.
suggested_refs: The Nicholas Gane interview with Haraway, academia.edu/4724092, source of the Hutchinson-and-cybernetics line, not fetched
sources: Research dossier's report of the Gane interview

stops.name: Woods Hole, the tunicates rebuilding themselves
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The UCSC finding aid and How Like a Leaf place her at the Marine Biological Laboratory summer course working on tunicate regeneration; the research pool tags the year [R] and the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory puts her at a bench on Cape Cod with tunicates, sea squirts that can be cut apart and will rebuild themselves. Regeneration is the problem: how a body knows what shape to return to when nobody has told it. Her dissertation will ask the same question in the archive rather than the tank, of biologists rather than of animals, and about metaphors rather than about tissue. She does no sustained laboratory work after this summer.
suggested_refs: The Marine Biological Laboratory summer course records, Woods Hole, 1968
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: New Haven, marriage to Jaye Miller
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The marriage and its year come from How Like a Leaf, Haraway's own autobiographical interview volume. No civil record was reached, and the New Haven placing follows the Yale milieu rather than a document. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: She marries Jaye Miller, a historian, in the Yale years. The marriage will not last as a marriage and will never stop being a family: they separate in three years, divorce without lawyers, and remain kin until his death. What she later calls kin is not a compromise reached after the fact. It is the arrangement itself, a household assembled out of former husbands, lovers, and friends who buy land together and hold it, and it outlasts the marriage by fifty years.
suggested_refs: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf, the sole source for the marriage and its dissolution
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: New Haven, the search for organizing relations
stops.date_confidence: attested. The UCSC finding aid and the Yale record give the 1972 Ph.D. in biology, the dissertation title, and G. Evelyn Hutchinson as adviser; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The doctorate is in biology and the thesis is a history of ideas: The Search for Organizing Relations, on the organismic paradigm in twentieth-century developmental biology, written under Hutchinson. She argues that biologists work through metaphors, that the metaphors are not decoration but apparatus, and that a field changes when its governing figure changes. It is the method she never afterward abandons. The committee passes it in 1972, and nobody at the time reads it as a manifesto.
suggested_refs: The 1972 Yale dissertation, The Search for Organizing Relations, revised four years later as her first book

segments.name: Honolulu and Baltimore: Becoming a Historian of Science

stops.name: Honolulu, general science at Manoa
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not resolved. Wikipedia, citing the European Graduate School, gives University of Hawai'i 1971-1974; Encyclopedia.com gives 1970-1974 as assistant professor of general science at the University of Hawaii at Honolulu. The General Science teaching is corroborated independently. The research pool's 'experimental New College' detail appears in no source reached, including the article the claim cites, and is not used here.
stops.campa: Jaye Miller takes a position in Hawai'i and Haraway goes with him, teaching general science at Manoa to undergraduates who are not going to be scientists. It is the first time she has to say what science is to people with no stake in defending it, and the first time she teaches biology as something with a history and a politics rather than a syllabus. She stays four years, on an island where the biology outside the classroom window is not the biology in the textbook. The sources put her arrival at 1971 or at 1970, and neither of them cites a record.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia.com's entry giving 1970-1974 and the general-science title, against the European Graduate School's 1971
sources: Wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', citing the European Graduate School

stops.name: Honolulu, the divorce without lawyers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Haraway's own first-person account in How Like a Leaf supplies the separation, the approximate year, and the detail that the divorce was transacted in Hawai'i without lawyers. No civil record was reached; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The marriage ends and the kinship does not. Miller is gay; the household reorganizes rather than dissolves; the divorce is transacted in Hawai'i between the two of them, with no lawyer in the room and no version of the story in which either of them is the injured party. The vocabulary for what they have made arrives thirty years later, in a book about dogs. For now there is no word for it. She keeps him, and later keeps his partner Bob Filomeno, inside the family she counts as hers.
stops.quote: There cannot be just one companion species; there have to be at least two to make one.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, The Companion Species Manifesto (Prickly Paradigm Press, 2003)
suggested_refs: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf, the sole source for the Hawai'i divorce
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: Baltimore, the history of science department
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia records the Johns Hopkins appointment as assistant professor in the history of science in 1974, held until the 1980 move to Santa Cruz. The month is an ordering device. The pin is inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Johns Hopkins coordinate.
stops.campa: Johns Hopkins hires her as an assistant professor in the history of science, which means she has formally left the discipline she was trained in. The department that hired her expects a historian of biology; what it is growing is a reader who treats scientific writing as literature without conceding that it is therefore untrue. She reads the primatologists and the embryologists as writers, tracking how a laboratory turns a body into data and a metaphor into a fact. She holds the post for six years.
suggested_refs: The Johns Hopkins history of science department of the 1970s, her first appointment outside biology

stops.name: Baltimore, Rusten Hogness
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year, reconstruction as to the circumstance. Wikipedia's infobox records the partnership with Rusten Hogness from 1975. The research pool's February month is unsupported by any source reached and is dropped; the story that he first audited one of her courses at Johns Hopkins comes from How Like a Leaf alone.
stops.campa: Rusten Hogness enters her life in Baltimore. By her own telling he first turned up auditing one of her courses, though no record outside her interview volume confirms it. He becomes her partner for the next fifty years and, in the arrangement she keeps insisting is ordinary, joins the same extended household that already contains her former husband. They will hold land in Sonoma County and a house in Santa Cruz. Where the two of them actually met rests on one book and her memory of it.
suggested_refs: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf, the only source for the audited course
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: Baltimore, Crystals, Fabrics, and Fields
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1976 Yale University Press publication as a revision of the dissertation (Wikipedia). The pin is Baltimore, where she was living and teaching, not New Haven, where the press sat; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Yale University Press brings out the dissertation as her first book, under a title naming three metaphors rather than a thesis: crystals, fabrics, fields. The argument is that organicist biologists in the twentieth century did their work through such images, and that the images did the thinking. Everything she publishes afterward is a variation on that claim, that the figure is the apparatus. Reviewers file the book as history of science. It sells modestly.
suggested_refs: Crystals, Fabrics, and Fields: Metaphors of Organicism in Twentieth-Century Developmental Biology (Yale University Press, 1976)

stops.name: Healdsburg, thirty acres and a collapsed house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The joint purchase by Haraway, Hogness, Miller, and Nick Paulina of roughly thirty acres containing a collapsed house is Haraway's own account in How Like a Leaf; the terms and the year appear in no public record reached and no deed was consulted. The pin is the town, not the parcel, and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Four people buy about thirty acres outside Healdsburg together: Haraway, Hogness, her former husband Miller, and Nick Paulina. No legal category covers what this household is. It is not a commune, not a marriage, not a co-op, and the deed does not say kin. She will spend the rest of her career arguing that the categories are the problem, and that people make relatives by working on something together. On the land is a house that has fallen down. They rebuild it.
suggested_refs: Sonoma County deed records for the Healdsburg parcel, not consulted; the purchase is known only from How Like a Leaf
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

segments.name: Santa Cruz: The History of Consciousness

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the first chair of its kind
stops.date_confidence: attested. The UCSC oral-history page and Wikipedia record the 1980 appointment in the History of Consciousness programme, described in UCSC's own material as probably the first tenured professorship in feminist theory in the United States; that superlative is the university's claim about itself. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The History of Consciousness programme at Santa Cruz gives her a post with no clear precedent: a tenured professorship in feminist theory, described by her own university as probably the first in the country. The superlative is the university's claim about itself. The programme has no departmental subject, which suits her, since she has spent a decade refusing to hold one. She will teach here for the rest of her working life, on a campus standing in a redwood forest above the Pacific.
suggested_refs: The UCSC Regional History Project oral history with Haraway, library.ucsc.edu/reg-hist/haraway

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the commission from the Socialist Review
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the commission and the political occasion: the manifesto appeared in Socialist Review no. 80 (1985), commissioned by the journal's West Coast collective after Reagan's election. No source reached dates the drafting, so the 1983 date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: The West Coast collective of the Socialist Review asks a group of feminists what socialist feminism should be under Reagan. Haraway's answer runs to more than forty pages and does not answer the question. Instead of a programme it offers a figure: the cyborg, a creature of the military and industrial laboratories the left is supposed to be against, claimed as the ancestor everybody on the left already has. She writes it as an argument with her own side.
stops.quote: Blasphemy has always seemed to require taking things very seriously.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, A Cyborg Manifesto (1985/1991), opening page
suggested_refs: Socialist Review no. 80 (1985), pp. 65-108, the essay's first printing

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the informatics of domination
stops.date_confidence: attested. A Manifesto for Cyborgs appeared in Socialist Review no. 80 (1985), pp. 65-108. Both quotations were verified verbatim this session against the archive.org transcription (item anarchy_Cyborg_Manifesto_Harroway). Spelling note: that printed text gives the forename as 'Michael'; the philosopher is Michel Foucault.
stops.campa: The essay names the system it is written against: the informatics of domination, a world reorganized so that bodies, work, and reproduction are all handled as code and can therefore be exchanged, rewritten, and priced. Michel Foucault had described power working on bodies through discipline and the management of populations. Haraway says the description arrived a generation late, dispatches it in a single clause, and keeps going, because the machines she is looking at do not merely discipline bodies. They translate them.
stops.quote: Michael Foucault's biopolitics is a flaccid premonition of cyborg politics, a very open field.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, A Cyborg Manifesto (1985/1991); the archive.org transcription prints the forename as 'Michael'
suggested_refs: The section of the manifesto headed 'The Informatics of Domination'
sources: archive.org, item anarchy_Cyborg_Manifesto_Harroway, Cyborg_Manifesto_Harroway_djvu.txt, fetched and read

stops.name: Santa Cruz, rather a cyborg than a goddess
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the text: the closing line of A Cyborg Manifesto, verified verbatim against the archive.org transcription. The June date is an ordering device inside the 1985 publication year.
stops.campa: The manifesto ends by refusing the other option on offer. Feminism in 1985 has a powerful strand looking for a lost matriarchy, a body before technology, a goddess, and the closing sentence turns it down in nine words that will be reprinted on posters and T-shirts for forty years. Haraway will not have it: there is no innocent nature to return to, the boundary between organism and machine has already been breached, and pretending otherwise concedes the laboratory to the people who own it.
stops.quote: Though both are bound in the spiral dance, I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, A Cyborg Manifesto (1985/1991), closing line
suggested_refs: Lynn Randolph's painting 'Cyborg' (1989), later the cover of Simians, Cyborgs, and Women

stops.name: Santa Cruz, situated knowledges
stops.date_confidence: attested: Feminist Studies 14, no. 3 (1988), pp. 575-599, JSTOR stable/3178066. The full text is paywalled and was not reached; the quotation was verified instead against the book reprint, Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (Routledge, 1991), ch. 9, p. 193, archive.org transcription, running head 'Situated Knowledges 193'. The research pool tagged this quotation [R]; it is upgraded to attested. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Three years after the cyborg she writes the essay answering the objection the cyborg invited. If all knowledge is made, in laboratories, by interested people, does anything remain true? Her answer is that objectivity is neither the view from nowhere nor a view from everywhere, but a view from somewhere specific, embodied, locatable, and therefore accountable. Partial perspective is not a defect to apologize for. It is the only condition under which a claim can be argued with.
stops.quote: Splitting, not being, is the privileged image for feminist epistemologies of scientific knowledge.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, 'Situated Knowledges,' in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (Routledge, 1991), ch. 9, p. 193
suggested_refs: Feminist Studies 14, no. 3 (1988), pp. 575-599, the essay's first printing, paywalled at JSTOR

stops.name: Healdsburg, the epidemic reaches the household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the pin is undocumented. Both deaths come from Haraway's first-person account in How Like a Leaf: Bob Filomeno, Jaye Miller's partner, of AIDS in 1986, and Miller of AIDS-related illness in 1991. No source reached gives a place for either death; the pin is the shared Sonoma County household rather than a documented location, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The epidemic reaches the household. Bob Filomeno, Jaye Miller's partner, dies of AIDS; five years later Miller dies too, the man Haraway married in New Haven and divorced in Honolulu and never stopped counting as family. She is writing, in those same years, about bodies as immune systems, about a self defined by what it recognizes as other, about a discourse in which the body is a battlefield and the enemy is inside. The theory and the funerals are running on the same calendar. She goes on calling both men kin after they are dead.
suggested_refs: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf, the only source for both deaths and for the kin network around them
sources: Haraway and Goodeve, How Like a Leaf

stops.name: Santa Cruz, Primate Visions
stops.date_confidence: attested: Routledge, 1989. The American Sociological Association's Science, Knowledge and Technology section gave the book its Robert K. Merton Award in 1992 (asanet.org award history). The pin is her own campus, where the work was done; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Primate Visions reads the twentieth century's monkey science as a story the West tells about itself: dioramas, field studies, National Geographic, the ape as the mirror in which race, sex, and origin get arranged. She does not accuse primatologists of lying. She shows that a discipline about human nature is bound to be built out of whatever its makers already believe human nature is. Some reviewers call it the most serious archival work done on the field. Others call it partisan and relativist, and say so in print.
suggested_refs: The American Museum of Natural History's Akeley Hall of African Mammals, the diorama sequence the book opens on
sources: asanet.org award-recipient history, Robert K. Merton Award 1992

stops.name: Santa Cruz, Simians, Cyborgs, and Women
stops.date_confidence: attested: Routledge, 1991, reprinting the 1985 Socialist Review essay under the title by which it is now universally known and 'Situated Knowledges' as chapter 9. The dedication carries her mother's dates. The quotation is verified against the archive.org transcription of the manifesto.
stops.campa: The collected essays put the manifesto between hard covers and give it the title everyone now uses. In this form it travels: to art schools, to architecture studios, to science fiction conventions, to Buenos Aires, into languages Haraway does not read. Its opening pages define the creature that follows her for the rest of her life, and that she will spend two decades explaining she never meant as a celebration of technology. The book is dedicated to Dorothy, dead thirty years.
stops.quote: A cyborg is a cybernetic organism, a hybrid of machine and organism, a creature of social reality as well as a creature of fiction.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, 'A Cyborg Manifesto,' in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (Routledge, 1991)
suggested_refs: Manifiesto para cyborgs (Puente Aereo, Buenos Aires, 2014), the Argentine edition of the essay
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Donna Haraway', for the Spanish editions

stops.name: Santa Cruz, Modest_Witness and the OncoMouse
stops.date_confidence: attested: Routledge, 1997, incorporating images by Lynn Randolph. The Society for Social Studies of Science gave the book its Ludwik Fleck Prize in 1999 (4sonline.org prize history). The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The title is an email address wearing a set of trademarks: Modest_Witness@Second_Millennium.FemaleMan(c)_Meets_OncoMouse(TM). The FemaleMan comes from Joanna Russ; the OncoMouse is a real animal, engineered to grow tumours and patented by Harvard, the first patented mammal. Haraway puts the two in one sentence to show that the laboratory now produces creatures that are simultaneously organisms, commodities, and characters. Lynn Randolph's paintings run through the book. The two women have been working together since Randolph painted the cyborg.
suggested_refs: Lynn Randolph's paintings for Modest_Witness, and her earlier 'Cyborg' (1989)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the prizes of a field she had been irritating
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the awards, unlocated as to ceremony. The Merton Award (ASA, 1992), the Ludwik Fleck Prize (4S, 1999), and the J. D. Bernal Prize for lifetime contribution (4S, September 2000) are all recorded by the awarding bodies. None of the sources reached says where Haraway was when any was conferred, so the pin is her own campus and the date is the Bernal award's month.
stops.campa: Within eight years the field she has been irritating gives her its three main honours: the sociologists give the Merton Award to Primate Visions, the science studies society gives the Fleck Prize to Modest_Witness, and then comes the Bernal, awarded for a life's work rather than for a book. She is fifty-six, and has thirty years of writing still in front of her. None of the sources reached says where any of the three was conferred, or whether she was in the room when it was.
suggested_refs: The 4S prize records at 4sonline.org for the Fleck Prize (1999) and the Bernal Prize (2000)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the second manifesto is a dog
stops.date_confidence: attested: Prickly Paradigm Press, Chicago, 2003, with the quotation verified against the archive.org transcription. The dog Cayenne Pepper is named in the earthlysurvival.org material on the 2016 documentary; the breed and the agility training come from the manifesto's own text. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Eighteen years after the cyborg she writes a second manifesto, and the creature this time is a dog. Coevolution is not a metaphor here: dogs and people made each other over thousands of years, in the flesh, and neither species can be described without the other. Cayenne Pepper is an Australian shepherd. On weekends the two of them run agility courses together, an amateur sport in which a human and a dog have to become legible to each other at speed, and Haraway takes it as an epistemological problem.
stops.quote: We are, constitutively, companion species. We make each other up, in the flesh.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, The Companion Species Manifesto (Prickly Paradigm Press, 2003)
suggested_refs: The Companion Species Manifesto: Dogs, People, and Significant Otherness (Prickly Paradigm Press, 2003)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, respect as a practice
stops.date_confidence: attested as to text, ordering as to date. The Haraway Reader appeared from Routledge in 2004; the quotation is from The Companion Species Manifesto (2003), verified against the archive.org transcription. The June date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Haraway Reader collects twenty years of essays for readers who arrived by way of the cyborg and have to be told there is more. What the recent work insists on is unfashionable in theory and ordinary in a training yard: that respect is a practice, that love without conditions is a fantasy and mostly a neurotic one, that the messy conditions are the point. She refuses to let the dogs become figures. They are not thinking material. They are animals she lives with and trains and will outlive.
stops.quote: Dogs are not surrogates for theory; they are not here just to think with. They are here to live with.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, The Companion Species Manifesto (Prickly Paradigm Press, 2003)
suggested_refs: The Haraway Reader (Routledge, 2004)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the contact zone
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not resolved. The University of Minnesota Press catalogue gives 26 November 2007 for the Posthumanities paperback, ISBN 9780816650460; the book is very widely catalogued and cited as 2008, the Vatican included, whose Laudate Deum cites 'D. J. HARAWAY, When Species Meet, Minneapolis, 2008, pp. 205-249' at note 41. Both dates are real. The pin is her own campus.
stops.campa: The book that comes out of the agility field asks what happens in the moment two animals of different species actually look at each other and have to work out what to do next. She borrows the phrase contact zone from colonial linguistics, where it names the place two languages meet and neither wins. Sixteen years later Pope Francis takes the phrase out of these pages for a letter to the world's Catholics about the climate. The footnote gives the page range, 205 to 249.

stops.name: Santa Cruz, Staying with the Trouble
stops.date_confidence: attested: Duke University Press, 2016. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: She proposes a name for the present that is neither the Anthropocene nor the Capitalocene: the Chthulucene, from the chthonic, the powers of the underground and the compost heap. Her argument against the other two names is that each makes a single agent, Man or Capital, the hero of a story about the end, and a story with one hero cannot be lived in. What she wants instead is a practice of staying put in the damage and making relatives across species while it goes on. Whether that is a politics or a consolation is the question her critics keep putting to her.
suggested_refs: Staying with the Trouble: Making Kin in the Chthulucene (Duke University Press, 2016)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the spider and the monster
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the quotation, unresolved as to the dispute. The disavowal is at Staying with the Trouble, p. 173, quoted verbatim by Sophie Lewis in Viewpoint, 8 May 2017, which was fetched and read this session; Lewis argues the disavowal fails because Pimoa cthulhu was itself named after Lovecraft's creature. The date orders the segment and the quarrel is live, not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: The name she chose comes from a spider, Pimoa cthulhu, which lives under the redwoods of her own coast, and from the chthonic earth-powers, and, she insists in a note, not from H. P. Lovecraft's tentacled god. She spells it differently on purpose. Critics point out that the arachnologist who described the spider named it after Lovecraft, so the horror writer's monster is inside her word whether she wants it there or not. The objection has not gone away, and neither has the term.
stops.quote: Cthulhu (note spelling), luxuriating in the science fiction of H.P. Lovecraft, plays no role for me, although it/he did play a role for Gustave Hormiga, the scientist who named my spider demon familiar.... I take the liberty of rescuing my spider from Lovecraft for other stories.
stops.quote_source: Donna Haraway, Staying with the Trouble (Duke University Press, 2016), p. 173, as quoted in Sophie Lewis, Viewpoint, 8 May 2017

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the two manifestos bound together
stops.date_confidence: attested: University of Minnesota Press, 2016, binding the 1985 and 2003 manifestos with a conversation with Cary Wolfe. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Minnesota binds the two manifestos into one volume with a long conversation between Haraway and Cary Wolfe at the end. Thirty-one years separate the cyborg from the dog, and the book asks her to say what they have in common. Her answer is that both are refusals of the individual: a cyborg is not one thing and a companion species is not one species, and in each case the unit that does the living is a relation rather than a body. The book appears in 2016. She is seventy-two.
suggested_refs: Manifestly Haraway (University of Minnesota Press, 2016), with the Cary Wolfe conversation

stops.name: Santa Cruz, making kin, not population
stops.date_confidence: attested: Prickly Paradigm Press, Chicago, 2018, coedited with Adele E. Clarke. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The book she edits with Adele Clarke takes the most combustible of her slogans and tries to argue it properly. Human numbers are a real pressure on a finite planet, and every previous attempt to say so has produced coercion aimed at poor and brown women. Haraway's position is that the demand has to be uncoupled from the coercion: fewer babies and more relatives, chosen and made and cared for, with the burden laid on the rich rather than the poor. She spends the following decade being misread on this in both directions.
suggested_refs: Making Kin Not Population, ed. Adele E. Clarke and Donna Haraway (Prickly Paradigm Press, 2018)

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the fall in the lemon tree
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Haraway tells the story herself in her Erasmus Prize acceptance speech (erasmusprijs.org). No source reached gives a date or a precise location; the research pool places it at her California home, the pin is the city of Santa Cruz, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: She trips while picking lemons at home, falls, and strikes her head. For months afterward she has trouble with balance and a ringing in her ears that will not stop. She is in her eighty-first year and prizes are arriving from two continents, and the thing that has actually happened to her is a lemon tree and a bad landing. She tells the story herself in a prize speech, in front of a foundation and a royal patron, because it is the kind of detail she has spent fifty years insisting belongs in the account. The imbalance and the tinnitus are still with her when she gives it.

stops.name: Santa Cruz, the painting with the machine in it
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, single-sourced. The research pool records an El Pais interview of 24 July 2026 in which Haraway describes herself as pro-child and non-natalist rather than anti-natalist and discusses artificial intelligence by way of a new Lynn Randolph painting joining a cyborg figure to Anthropic's Claude. stops.campa: At eighty-one she is still correcting the record: not anti-natalist, she says, pro-child and non-natalist, a distinction she has been drawing for forty years and which almost nobody transcribes correctly. Lynn Randolph, who painted the cyborg on the 1991 cover, has made a new picture joining that figure to a language model. Haraway looks at the machines the way she looked at the OncoMouse and the sea squirt: as a kind of relative that somebody built, and that somebody owns.
